newsitem.title: INDIA: India plans to seek bids for ports' privatisation.
newsitem.headline: India plans to seek bids for ports' privatisation.

text.p: India is considering inviting bids for privatising at least 21 port operations, involving an investment of $6.59 billion in the next two years, a senior government official told Reuters on Thursday.

"We are encouraging more and more private investment for three reasons - lack of adequate resources, better management expertise and better technology," said Pankaj Jain, director (ports development) in the Surface Transport Ministry.

The ministry has submitted recommendations listing construction of modern terminals and outer harbours, multipurpose berths and drydock facitlities among the projects that should be offered to private investment.
India, under an ambitious economic reforms programme launched in 1991, threw open its ports sector for private and foreign investment.
Private investment is involved in at least 25 port projects such as leasing, construction and handling of berths, creation of storage facilities and building of container terminals.
Jain said bids were currently invited for privatising the multipurpose jetty at the New Mangalore port and container handling berths at the Tuticorin port.
India currently allows automatic foreign equity approval up to 74 percent in most port operations subject to guidelines.
Jain said companies from South Korea, Japan, the United States, Malaysia, Singapore, the United Kingdom and Netherlands had shown interest in investing in India's ports.
"We expect that there will be good foreign participation, especially in container terminal ventures," Jain said. "We also want to borrow from their experience."
Jain said the government was trying to clear private investment proposals quickly as it was necessary for both export and for the development of ports.
He said the surface transport ministry had also planned to boost the port handling capacity in the next five years to 424 million tonnes by adding a new capacity of 172 million.
"An investment of 152 billion rupees ($4.25 billion) will be required to create the additional capacity," Jain said.
"But also with this kind of investment, we will be able to create an additional capacity to the extent of only 122 million tonnes," Jain said.
"We will still be falling short of creating the targeted capacity by 50 million tonnes," he said, adding it was expected to be generated by building new harbours.
Of the total investment planned, 88 billion rupees would come from public sector agencies and 64 billion from the private sector, he said.
"We are encouraging foreign investment and we are expecting large foreign participation in port operations," Jain said.
India has 11 major ports and 139 minor ports along its 5,560 km (3,475 miles) coastline, which together handles about 90 percent of the country's foreign trade. The rest is by air.
Indian ports handled 229 million tonnes in 1996/97 (April/March) against a capacity of 215 million, which in the current year is expected to go up to 252 million.
He said the privatisation programme for ports had been taken up keeping in view the interests of port workers.
"The guidelines have been so framed that there will no adverse impact on the port labourers," Jain said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
